content: Loa loa filariasis is a disease affecting the skin and eyes, caused by the nematode worm Loa loa. Humans acquire this infection through the bite of a horsefly, with the deer fly and mango fly also serving as vectors. The disease manifests as red, itchy swellings beneath the skin, known as Calabar swellings. The first documented case of Loa loa infection occurred in Santo Domingo in 1770. In 1895, localized angioedema, a hallmark symptom of loiasis, was observed in Calabar, a coastal town in Nigeria, giving rise to the term Calabar swellings. However, the connection between Loa loa and these swellings was not established until 1910 by Dr. Patrick Manson. Loiasis is caused by the nematode Loa loa, which resides in the lymphatic and subcutaneous tissues of humans. Adult worms are sexually dimorphic, with males measuring 30–34 mm in length and 0.35–0.42 mm in width, while females are larger, measuring 40–70 mm in length and 0.5 mm in width. These adult worms inhabit the subcutaneous tissues, where they mate and produce microfilariae. The microfilariae are 250–300 μm long and 6–8 μm wide, and they can be identified morphologically by their sheath and the presence of nuclei extending to the tip of the tail. The Loa loa parasite is endemic to West and Central Africa, with its geographical range extending from southeastern Benin to southern Sudan and Uganda in an east-west direction, and from approximately 10°N latitude to Angola in a north-south direction. It is estimated that 3 to 13 million people in these regions are infected. Individuals most at risk for loiasis are those living in the high-canopied rainforests of West and Central Africa. The deerflies that transmit the parasite are diurnal and are more prevalent during the rainy season. These flies are attracted to human movement and smoke from wood fires. Rubber plantations, with their dense tree canopies, provide an ideal environment for these flies. Symptoms of loiasis include itchy, non-painful swellings (Calabar swellings) that can occur anywhere on the body, often near joints. Less common symptoms include generalized itching, muscle pain, joint pain, and fatigue. Some infected individuals may remain asymptomatic. Diagnosing loiasis can be challenging, particularly in patients with low levels of microfilariae in the blood. Diagnosis is often initiated when a patient presents with an eye worm, Calabar swellings, or unexplained elevated eosinophil levels following travel to an endemic area. Confirmation can be achieved by identifying an adult worm removed from under the skin or eye, observing an adult worm in the eye during examination, detecting microfilariae in a blood smear collected between 10 AM and 2 PM, or identifying antibodies against Loa loa. Treatment for loiasis typically involves chemotherapy or, in some cases, surgical removal of adult worms followed by systemic therapy. The drug of choice is diethylcarbamazine (DEC), administered at a dose of 8–10 mg/kg/day, divided into three doses daily for 12 days. The pediatric dosage is the same. DEC is effective against microfilariae and has some efficacy against adult worms. However, in patients with a high microfilarial load, DEC may be contraindicated due to the risk of encephalopathy caused by the rapid killing of microfilariae. In such cases, albendazole has been found to be a safer alternative and is more effective than ivermectin, which also carries risks despite its slower action. Surgical removal of migrating adult worms is an effective treatment for localized symptoms and provides an opportunity for diagnosis. However, systemic therapy is required to fully eradicate the infection unless the patient harbors only a single adult worm. There are currently no vaccines available to prevent Loa loa infection. Weekly prophylactic administration of DEC (300 mg) is effective for long-term travelers to endemic areas. Avoiding areas where deerflies breed, such as muddy, shaded regions along rivers, and staying away from wood fire smoke can reduce the risk of infection.
